# Interpreting the Decision Tree: When and Why Cytoplasmic Actin Drives pERK Prediction

## 1. What the Tree Is Actually Telling Us

Because Class 1 = cells in the extreme 10% of **positive Integrated Gradients attribution of Cytoplasm Intensity mean Actin to pERK**, the tree is not predicting pERK itself — it is identifying the **cellular states in which actin becomes the dominant explanatory variable for ERK activation**. The feature hierarchy reads as a mechanistic cascade:

| Tier | Split feature | Biological meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Root (1.106, 1.342, 2.170) | **Cytoplasmic Paxillin** | Focal adhesion (FA) abundance — the *gate* |
| Second | **Nuclear YAP** | Mechanotransduction/Hippo state — the *gain controller* |
| Third | **Cytobody Paxillin / Nuclear DAPI** | FA maturation & distribution / cell-cycle context — the *refiners* |

The critical pattern is a **graded Paxillin–YAP trade-off**: low paxillin requires very high nuclear YAP to rescue high actin attribution (Node 14: YAP > 0.586, weak 51.8%); intermediate paxillin needs YAP > 0.331 (Nodes 29/30); high paxillin (>1.342) needs only YAP > −0.236 (Nodes 27/28); and extreme paxillin (>2.170) abolishes the YAP requirement entirely (Node 24). This compensation logic suggests both features feed a **shared currency — adhesion-coupled cytoskeletal tension — through which actin licenses sustained ERK signaling**.

## 2. Robustness Ranking of Target Zones

| Rank | Node | TP | FP | Precision | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 (Primary)** | **28** | **248** | 30 | **89.2%** | High paxillin + nuclear YAP + high cytobody paxillin |
| **2 (Secondary)** | **24** | 38 | 4 | **90.5%** | Extreme paxillin + nuclear YAP depleted |
| Supporting | 27 | 190 | 69 | 73.4% | Sibling of 28 (same parent; combined 438 TP, 81.6%) |
| Supporting | 23 | 242 | 196 | 55.3% | Same branch as 24 — purifies only at paxillin > 2.17 |

Nodes 28 and 24 represent **two mechanistically distinct regimes** and are analyzed separately below.

---

## 3. PRIMARY ZONE — Node 28 (TP = 248, Precision = 89.2%)

**Logic:** Cytoplasmic Paxillin > 1.342 **AND** Nuclear YAP > −0.236 **AND** Cytobody Paxillin > 1.597
**Plain language:** In well-spread, strongly adherent cells with abundant paxillin-rich focal adhesions distributed across the cell body and active nuclear YAP, cytoplasmic actin intensity is almost always the top positive driver of predicted pERK.

### 3.1 Findings that directly confirm established literature

1. **Focal adhesions gate the actin→pERK relationship.** The root split on paxillin confirms that actin only predicts ERK activity when anchored to integrin adhesions. FAK autophosphorylation (Y397) recruits Src, which phosphorylates FAK-Y925 and paxillin (Y31/Y118), creating Grb2–SOS docking sites that feed directly into Ras–ERK (Schlaepfer et al., *Nature* 1994; Turner, *Nat Cell Biol* 2000). Growth-factor and integrin signals are known to be obligatorily synergistic for MAPK activation (Miyamoto et al., *J Cell Biol* 1996; Moro et al., *EMBO J* 1998), and actin cytoskeletal integrity is required for *sustained* ERK activity (Aplin & Juliano, *J Cell Sci* 1999; Roovers et al., *Mol Biol Cell* 1999). The tree recapitulates this anchorage dependence *in silico*: without paxillin > 1.106, virtually no high-attribution cells exist.
2. **The positive actin–pERK correlation reflects a known positive feedback loop.** ERK phosphorylates myosin light chain kinase to drive actomyosin contractility (Klemke et al., *J Cell Biol* 1997), phosphorylates paxillin at Ser83 to remodel adhesions (Ishibe et al., *Mol Cell* 2004; Liu et al., *J Biol Chem* 2002), and phosphorylates cortactin to promote Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly (Martinez-Quiles et al., *Mol Cell Biol* 2004). Actin density and pERK therefore reinforce each other — exactly the positive correlation observed.
3. **Nuclear YAP co-occurrence is expected.** Actin tension and adhesion strength mechanically open nuclear pores to drive YAP nuclear import (Dupont et al., *Nature* 2011; Elosegui-Artola et al., *Cell* 2017). High-paxillin/high-actin cells *should* be YAP-nuclear — and they are.

### 3.2 New, experimentally testable hypotheses

- **H1 — Focal adhesion *maturation state* encodes ERK coupling strength.** The sibling split (Node 27 vs 28) shows that concentrating paxillin in the cell body (cytobody > 1.597) raises precision from 73.4% → 89.2% and adds 58 TP. *Hypothesis:* mature, centrally located, tension-bearing adhesions sustain ERK longer than peripheral nascent adhesions. **Test:** co-stain paxillin with pFAK-Y397 and pPaxillin-Y118 after 10 ng/mL EGF; measure ERK pulse duration with an ERK-KTR live biosensor (Regot et al., *Cell* 2014); perturb with FAK inhibitor (defactinib), blebbistatin, or ML-7 and quantify loss of actin attribution in Node 28-like cells.
- **H2 — YAP is a transcriptional gain amplifier of the actin–adhesion–ERK circuit.** YAP/TAZ activity itself controls focal adhesion assembly and cell mechanics (Nardone et al., *Nat Commun* 2017), and EGF acutely activates YAP via PI3K–PDK1–LATS (Fan et al., *PNAS* 2013). *Hypothesis:* nuclear YAP raises paxillin/actin levels, which in turn strengthens actin's contribution to pERK — a slow feed-forward loop layered on the fast ERK feedback. **Test:** YAP/TAZ siRNA or verteporfin (TEAD inhibition) should selectively blunt EGF-induced pERK in high-paxillin cells; constitutively active YAP-5SA should convert Node 27-like cells into Node 28-like states.
- **H3 — A quantitative "mechanochemical load" threshold.** *Hypothesis:* traction stress, not paxillin per se, is the causal variable; Node 28 cells sit above a tension threshold. **Test:** traction force microscopy stratified by tree zone; softening the substrate should move cells out of Node 28 and collapse the actin→pERK attribution.

---

## 4. SECOND ZONE — Node 24 (TP = 38, Precision = 90.5%)

**Logic:** Cytoplasmic Paxillin > 2.170 **AND** Nuclear YAP ≤ −0.236
**Plain language:** A rare but extremely pure subpopulation: cells with *saturated* cytoplasmic paxillin (>2.17 SD above mean) in which nuclear YAP is below average — yet actin remains a top pERK driver in 90.5% of cases. Its sibling Node 23 (paxillin 1.342–2.170, same YAP-depleted branch) achieves only 55.3% precision despite 242 TP, indicating a **sharp paxillin dose threshold** for YAP-independent coupling.

### 4.1 Findings that directly confirm established literature

1. **Saturated adhesion scaffolding is sufficient for ERK activation.** At extreme integrin/FA density, FAK–Grb2–SOS and paxillin scaffolding can maintain Ras–ERK signaling without additional mechanotranscriptional input — consistent with classic integrin–EGFR synergy being fundamentally dose-dependent on receptor/integrin occupancy (Miyamoto et al., 1996; Moro et al., 1998; Schlaepfer et al., 1994).
2. **YAP is parallel to, not obligatory for, MAPK signaling.** Hippo/YAP and Ras/ERK are separable modules that cross-regulate but do not require each other (Hansen et al., *Trends Cell Biol* 2015; Zanconato et al., *Cancer Cell* 2016). The tree confirms ERK coupling can persist in YAP-low cells.

### 4.2 New, experimentally testable hypotheses

- **H4 — Ultrasensitive adhesion–ERK coupling.** The jump from 55.3% (Node 23) to 90.5% (Node 24) across paxillin ≈ 2.17 suggests cooperativity (adhesion clustering → signalosome formation). **Test:** dose-response of pERK amplitude/duration (ERK-KTR) vs. quantified paxillin intensity and pPaxillin-Y118 across the 2.17 boundary; test whether partial FAK inhibition shifts the threshold rightward.
- **H5 — Cytoplasmic YAP may be recruited into the adhesion compartment.** Nuclear YAP ≤ −0.236 implies cytoplasmic retention (pYAP-S127/LATS-active state). *Hypothesis:* in adhesion-saturated cells, cytoplasmic YAP localizes near focal adhesions and participates in adhesion–ERK cross-talk, or YAP export is itself a downstream consequence of strong ERK activity (negative feedback). **Test:** multiplexed imaging of total YAP, pYAP-S127, and pLATS co-registered with paxillin; dual ERK-KTR + YAP live-cell reporters during EGF stimulation to order events temporally; LATS1/2 inhibition should test whether forcing YAP nuclear entry converts Node 24 cells toward the Node 28 phenotype and whether actin attribution changes.
- **H6 — Two redundant circuits converge on ERK.** *Hypothesis:* cells use either a YAP-coupled circuit (Node 28) or an adhesion-saturated circuit (Node 24) to sustain ERK; blocking one reroutes cells to the other. **Test:** combined YAP inhibition + partial adhesion disruption (low-dose latrunculin B or FAK inhibitor) should synergistically abolish pERK, whereas single perturbations should only shift cells between zones.

---

## 5. Supporting Evidence from Remaining Zones

- **Node 27** (190 TP, 73.4%) — same parent as Node 28; confirms the high-paxillin/YAP-positive regime is robust even before the cytobody-paxillin refinement.
- **Nodes 29/30** (paxillin 1.106–1.342, YAP > 0.331) — the DAPI split (59.2% → 71.5% precision) suggests **cell-cycle/DNA-content modulation** of actin–pERK coupling, consistent with cell-cycle regulation of ERK (Liu et al., *Oncogene* 2004; Aoki et al., *Mol Cell* 2013). Testable via FUCCI/synchronization.
- **Node 14** (weakest, 51.8%) — extreme YAP (>0.586) only partially compensates for low paxillin, reinforcing that **adhesion is the primary gate and YAP the secondary tuner**.

## 6. Integrated Model

EGF (10 ng/mL) triggers EGFR→Ras→ERK pulses (Albeck et al., *Mol Cell* 2013), but the *persistence* of pERK — and hence actin's power to predict it — is set by a mechanochemical scaffold: **paxillin-rich focal adhesions anchor actin stress fibers (gate), actomyosin tension drives YAP nuclear entry and YAP-dependent reinforcement of adhesion genes (gain), and cell-body adhesion maturation plus cell-cycle state fine-tune the coupling (refiners).** ERK closes the loop by phosphorylating MLCK, paxillin-S83, and cortactin. Actin is the physical integrator of this circuit, which is why its attribution to pERK concentrates in Node 28 (YAP-coupled) and Node 24 (adhesion-saturated) cells.

**Caveats:** thresholds are z-score landmarks from a depth-4 tree; IG attribution reflects model reliance, not causation; Node 24 (n=42) requires validation given its small size.

## 7. Key Publications

1. Schlaepfer DD et al. *Nature* 372:786–791 (1994) — FAK–Grb2–Ras–MAPK linkage.
2. Miyamoto S et al. *J Cell Biol* 135:1633–1642 (1996) — integrin–growth factor synergy for MAPK.
3. Moro L et al. *EMBO J* 17:6622–6632 (1998) — integrin-mediated EGFR transactivation.
4. Aplin AE, Juliano RL. *J Cell Sci* 112:695–706 (1999) — cytoskeletal regulation of growth-factor→MAPK.
5. Roovers K et al. *Mol Biol Cell* 10:3197–3204 (1999) — sustained ERK requires α5β1 integrin.
6. Klemke RL et al. *J Cell Biol* 137:481–492 (1997) — ERK phosphorylates MLCK.
7. Ishibe S et al. *Mol Cell* 16:257–267 (2004) — paxillin as ERK-regulated scaffold (Ser83).
8. Liu ZX et al. *J Biol Chem* 277:10452–10458 (2002) — ERK-dependent paxillin phosphorylation in epithelia.
9. Martinez-Quiles N et al. *Mol Cell Biol* 24:5269–5280 (2004) — ERK/Src–cortactin–N-WASP actin control.
10. Turner CE. *Nat Cell Biol* 2:E231–E236 (2000) — paxillin signaling review.
11. Dupont S et al. *Nature* 474:179–183 (2011) — YAP/TAZ mechanotransduction.
12. Elosegui-Artola A et al. *Cell* 171:1397–1410 (2017) — force-gated YAP nuclear import.
13. Nardone G et al. *Nat Commun* 8:15321 (2017) — YAP controls focal adhesion assembly.
14. Fan R, Kim NG, Gumbiner BM. *PNAS* 110:2569–2574 (2013) — mitogens/EGF regulate YAP via PI3K–PDK1.
15. Regot S et al. *Cell* 157:1724–1734 (2014) — KTR biosensors for live ERK/YAP dynamics.
16. Albeck JG, Mills GB, Brugge JS. *Mol Cell* 49:249–261 (2013) — EGF-driven ERK pulse dynamics.
17. Liu X et al. *Oncogene* 23:763–776 (2004) — MAPK requirement at G2/M (DAPI-zone rationale).
18. Hansen CG, Moroishi T, Guan KL. *Trends Cell Biol* 25:499–513 (2015) — YAP/TAZ–MAPK cross-talk framework.

# Interpretation of Decision Tree Zones: Conditional Coupling of Cytoplasmic Actin to pERK in EGF-Stimulated Mammary Epithelial Cells

## 1. Global Logic of the Tree

The tree does **not** treat Actin→pERK attribution as a uniform property of all cells. Instead, it asks: *in which cellular states does cytoplasmic F-actin become a dominant predictor of pERK?* The answer is carved out almost entirely by **two variables — cytoplasmic Paxillin (root split, and 3 of 4 levels) and nuclear YAP** — with secondary refinement by Cytobody Paxillin and DAPI. This defines a compensatory threshold surface:

- **Paxillin ≤ 1.106** → virtually no high-attribution cells (entire left subtree is Class 0 except Node 14 at 51.8%).
- **Paxillin > 1.106** → the required "extra condition" relaxes as paxillin rises: moderate paxillin needs high nuclear YAP (Nodes 29/30); high paxillin needs only baseline YAP (Nodes 27/28); **extreme paxillin needs no YAP at all** (Node 24).

This is the signature of a **coincidence-detection / partial-redundancy architecture**: focal adhesion abundance (Paxillin) and mechanotranscriptional activity (nuclear YAP) are additive inputs into the strength of Actin–ERK coupling.

## 2. Zone Robustness Ranking

| Rank | Node | TP | FP | Precision | Cellular state |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **28** | **248** | 30 | **89.2%** | High Paxillin + nuclear YAP + high Cytobody Paxillin |
| **2** | **24** | 38 | 4 | **90.5%** | Extreme Paxillin (>2.17) + YAP excluded |
| 3 | 27 | 190 | 69 | 73.4% | High Paxillin + nuclear YAP, moderate Cytobody Paxillin |
| 4 | 30 | 103 | 41 | 71.5% | Moderate Paxillin + high YAP + high DAPI |
| 5 | 29 | 42 | 29 | 59.2% | Moderate Paxillin + high YAP + low DAPI |
| 6 | 23 | 242 | 196 | 55.3% | High Paxillin + low YAP (sub-threshold) |
| 7 | 14 | 101 | 94 | 51.8% | Low-moderate Paxillin + high YAP |

**Node 28 is the primary zone** (largest TP count *and* near-top precision; n=278, statistically robust). **Node 24 is the second zone** (highest precision in the tree, small n → hypothesis-generating, and biologically complementary because it is YAP-*negative*). Node 27 serves as an internal dose-control for Node 28 (identical parent branch; raising Cytobody Paxillin past 1.597 raises precision 73.4%→89.2%).

---

## 3. PRIMARY ZONE — Node 28
**Logic:** Cytoplasm Paxillin > 1.342 **AND** Nucleus YAP > −0.236 **AND** Cytobody Paxillin > 1.597
**TP = 248, Precision = 89.2%**

### Biological rationale

These are well-spread, strongly adherent cells with abundant/mature focal adhesions (FAs) and retained nuclear YAP — i.e., a **mechanically engaged state**. In this state, cytoplasmic actin becomes the top predictor of pERK because F-actin is simultaneously:

1. **The structural substrate of an ERK signaling platform.** Integrin engagement → FAK autophosphorylation (Y397) → Src recruitment → paxillin phosphorylation (Y31/Y118) → Grb2/SOS → Ras→Raf→MEK→ERK. EGFR→ERK signaling is strongly adhesion-dependent, so cells with high paxillin convert EGF input into larger pERK output. More F-actin = more/mature FAs = more docking sites.
2. **A physical scaffold for the kinase cascade itself.** Paxillin is an ERK-regulated scaffold (ERK phosphorylates paxillin at Ser126, creating a paxillin–ERK association); the actin-binding protein IQGAP1 scaffolds Raf–MEK–ERK on F-actin. Actin intensity therefore *linearly reports scaffolded ERK capacity*.
3. **The actuator of a YAP→AREG→EGFR feedforward loop.** Actomyosin tension drives YAP nuclear translocation; in MCF10A cells YAP/TEAD induces **amphiregulin (AREG)**, an autocrine EGFR ligand that sustains pERK. ERK then remodels actin (WAVE2, MLCK, paxillin-S126), closing a positive feedback loop — which explains the observed **positive Actin–pERK correlation**.

### Category 1 — Findings that directly confirm published knowledge
- **Focal adhesion abundance gates ERK amplitude** (Paxillin as root split; Class 1 nearly absent below Paxillin 1.106): canonical integrin–FAK–Grb2–Ras–ERK signaling and anchorage-dependent ERK (Schlaepfer et al., 1994; Giancotti & Ruoslahti, 1999; Howe et al., 2002; Aplin & Juliano, 1999).
- **Integrin–EGFR crosstalk**: integrin ligation transactivates EGFR and is required for full MAPK induction (Moro et al., 1998).
- **Paxillin–ERK scaffolding** in epithelial morphogenesis (Ishibe et al., 2003, 2004).
- **Nuclear YAP marks stress-fiber-rich, mechanically engaged cells** (Dupont et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2011; Aragona et al., 2013).
- **YAP→AREG→EGFR autocrine amplification in MCF10A** (Zhang et al., 2009); growth-factor (EGF) control of YAP via PI3K/PDK1 and EGFR–MAPK→YAP crosstalk (Fan et al., 2013; Reddy & Irvine, 2013).
- **ERK→actin feedback** (Mendoza et al., 2011; Klemke et al., 1997).
- Consistent with tension→integrin/ERK phenotypes in mammary epithelium (Paszek et al., 2005; Levental et al., 2009) and with multiplexed single-cell designs linking subcellular organization to signaling states (Gut et al., 2018).

### Category 2 — New testable hypotheses
- **H1 (AND-gate):** Actin→pERK attribution requires *both* high Paxillin and nuclear YAP (Nodes 14 and 23 alone are ~52–55% pure). *Test:* FAK inhibition (PF-562271), YAP/TEAD inhibition (verteporfin/CRISPR), or low-dose latrunculin B in EGF-stimulated cells; predict collapse of Actin–pERK conditional mutual information only when **either** input is removed from Node-28-state cells.
- **H2 (FA maturation threshold):** The Cytobody-Paxillin 1.597 gate (73.4%→89.2%) suggests force-dependent FA maturation licenses ERK scaffolding. *Test:* vinculin FRET tension sensor + FA lifetime imaging; proximity ligation of pERK–paxillin; predict pERK enrichment at mature (tension-bearing) FAs.
- **H3 (feedforward bistability):** The Actin→YAP→AREG→EGFR→ERK→actin loop predicts hysteresis in pERK after EGF pulses. *Test:* AREG-neutralizing antibody or gefitinib wash-in after EGF; predict selective loss of *sustained* (not peak) pERK in Node-28-state cells.
- **H4 (IQGAP1 link):** IQGAP1 knockdown should decouple Actin intensity from pERK without reducing either individually.

**Key publications:** Schlaepfer et al., *Nature* 1994; Moro et al., *EMBO J* 1998; Giancotti & Ruoslahti, *Science* 1999; Howe et al., *Curr Opin Genet Dev* 2002; Ishibe et al., *Mol Cell* 2003 & 2004; Roy, Li & Sacks, *JBC* 2004; Dupont et al., *Nature* 2011; Wada et al., *Development* 2011; Aragona et al., *Cell* 2013; Zhang et al., *Nat Cell Biol* 2009; Fan et al., *PNAS* 2013; Reddy & Irvine, *Dev Cell* 2013; Mendoza et al., *Mol Cell* 2011; Klemke et al., *JCB* 1997; Paszek et al., *Cancer Cell* 2005; Levental et al., *Cell* 2009; Gut et al., *Science* 2018.

---

## 4. SECOND ZONE — Node 24
**Logic:** Cytoplasm Paxillin > 2.170 **AND** Nucleus YAP ≤ −0.236
**TP = 38, FP = 4, Precision = 90.5%**

### Biological rationale

Compared with its sibling Node 23 (Paxillin 1.342–2.170, same YAP-low branch, precision only 55.3%), crossing **Paxillin > 2.17** purifies high attribution to 90.5%. This is a small (n=42) but ultra-pure state in which **Actin–pERK coupling persists without nuclear YAP**. Two non-exclusive interpretations:

1. **Adhesion-density saturation (YAP-independent, post-translational route).** At extreme FA density, integrin→FAK/Src→Grb2→Ras flux alone is sufficient to make the actin–adhesion machinery the rate-reporting variable for pERK; the YAP transcriptional amplifier is dispensable. Note that FA *number* does not equal FA *tension* — cells can be paxillin-high yet YAP-low (e.g., contact-inhibited/crowded, or low contractility), which cleanly separates "adhesion scaffold load" from "mechanotransduction output."
2. **High FA-turnover/motility state.** High *cytoplasmic* (non-adhesion-localized) paxillin can reflect ERK-driven FA disassembly: EGF→ERK activates calpain and ERK-dependent FAK Ser910 phosphorylation targets calpain to FAs, releasing paxillin during turnover. Migrating cells would then show tight Actin–pERK co-variation because both are locked into the same protrusion–adhesion–disassembly cycle.

### Category 1 — Findings that directly confirm published knowledge
- Extreme paxillin → FAK–Grb2–Ras–ERK is sufficient for MAPK activation (Schlaepfer et al., 1994; Mitra et al., 2005); canonical EGFR→Ras→ERK does not require YAP (Lemmon & Schlessinger, 2010).
- ERK localizes to and remodels FAs: paxillin–ERK association (Ishibe et al., 2003, 2004); ERK→FAK/calpain FA-disassembly axis (Carragher et al., 2003; Glading et al., 2004).
- YAP nuclear exclusion despite high adhesion is compatible with crowding/contact inhibition and cytoskeleton-dependent Hippo regulation (Dupont et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2012).

### Category 2 — New testable hypotheses
- **H1 (two-circuit model):** Actin–ERK coupling has two separable mechanical circuits — a *tension/YAP-dependent transcriptional circuit* (Node 28) and an *adhesion-density/turnover-dependent post-translational circuit* (Node 24). *Test:* YAP knockout or TEAD inhibition should spare Node-24-state coupling but shrink Node-28-state coupling; FAK inhibition should abolish both; blebbistatin should collapse YAP nuclear entry (Node 28) while leaving extreme-paxillin ERK coupling partially intact.
- **H2 (turnover coupling):** In this state, pERK should track FA *disassembly rate* rather than FA number. *Test:* live paxillin-GFP + ERK biosensor (EKAR/KTR; Regot et al., 2014) ± calpeptin/ALLN; predict calpain inhibition reduces pERK specifically in paxillin-extreme, YAP-low cells.
- **H3 (engineered state):** Micropatterned islands of varying size/adhesiveness to generate YAP-low/Paxillin-high cells; predict preserved EGF→pERK responses and preserved Actin attribution, confirming YAP-independence.
- **H4 (nonlinear threshold at 2.17):** Suggests cooperative FA clustering or receptor cross-activation. *Test:* titrate RGD ligand density/adhesion area and measure switch-like pERK responses.

**Key publications:** Schlaepfer et al., *Nature* 1994; Mitra et al., *Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol* 2005; Ishibe et al., *Mol Cell* 2003, 2004; Carragher et al., *Curr Biol* 2003; Glading et al., *Mol Cell Biol* 2004; Turner, *Nat Cell Biol* 2000; Grashoff et al., *Nature* 2010; Lemmon & Schlessinger, *Cell* 2010; Zhao et al., *Genes Dev* 2012; Regot et al., *Cell* 2014.

---

## 5. Supporting Context and Caveats

- **Node 14** (YAP-high, Paxillin low-moderate, 51.8%) and **Node 23** (Paxillin-high, YAP-low, 55.3%) are the critical negative contrasts: *neither input alone is sufficient* — the core evidence for the AND-gate.
- **Nodes 29/30** (moderate Paxillin, high YAP, split on DAPI): precision rises 59.2%→71.5% with DAPI > 0.307 (higher DNA content, S/G2), suggesting **cell-cycle modulation** of Actin–ERK coupling (Meloche & Pouysségur, *Oncogene* 2007).
- **Caveats:** thresholds are z-scored (population-relative); IG attribution is associational, not causal — the tree identifies states where Actin is *informative*, not proof that actin activates ERK; Node 24 (n=42) requires out-of-sample validation; a fixed post-EGF timepoint cannot resolve ERK pulse dynamics, which the proposed live-biosensor experiments address.

**Bottom line:** The tree resolves *why* cytoplasmic Actin predicts pERK: actin is the shared physical substrate of (i) focal-adhesion ERK scaffolding (Paxillin-gated) and (ii) YAP-mediated mechanotranscriptional amplification (YAP-gated). Node 28 captures the canonical, high-flux coincidence state; Node 24 reveals a rarer, YAP-independent extreme-adhesion bypass — together predicting a two-circuit, logic-gated architecture of EGF→ERK signaling in human breast epithelial cells.

# Interpretation of Decision Tree Logic: Gating of Actin→pERK Attribution by Focal Adhesion State and YAP Mechanotransduction

## 1. Global Logic of the Tree

The tree asks: *under what cellular state does Cytoplasmic Actin intensity become a dominant predictor of pERK?* The answer is unambiguous in structure:

- **Root + dominant splits: Cytoplasmic Paxillin** (focal adhesion load) — the master gate.
- **Secondary split: Nuclear YAP** (mechanotransduction/transcriptional state) — the modifier.
- **Tertiary splits: Cytobody Paxillin** (whole-cell adhesion density refinement) or **Nuclear DAPI** (cell-cycle proxy).

This means the Actin–pERK coupling is **not constitutive** — it is *conditionally licensed* by focal adhesion maturation, and further sharpened by YAP localization. This is a classic interaction effect that the MLP captured and the tree recovered.

**Zone ranking (by TP × Precision):**

| Rank | Node | TP | FP | Precision | Cellular state |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **28** | **248** | 30 | **89.2%** | High Paxillin + YAP nuclear + high Cytobody Paxillin |
| **2** | **24** | 38 | 4 | **90.5%** | Extreme Paxillin (>2.17) + YAP excluded |
| 3 | 27 | 190 | 69 | 73.4% | High Paxillin + YAP nuclear + moderate Cytobody Paxillin |
| 4 | 23 | 242 | 196 | 55.3% | High Paxillin (1.34–2.17) + YAP excluded |
| 5 | 30 | 103 | 41 | 71.5% | Moderate Paxillin + high YAP + high DAPI (G2-like) |

**Critical internal-consistency signal:** precision rises monotonically with Paxillin dose in *both* YAP branches (Node 27→28: 73.4%→89.2% as Cytobody Paxillin rises; Node 23→24: 55.3%→90.5% as Cytoplasmic Paxillin rises). A monotonic dose-dependent sharpening is the signature of a real biological gradient, not tree overfitting.

---

## 2. PRIMARY ZONE — Node 28 (TP=248, Precision=89.2%)

**Logic:** Cytoplasm Paxillin > 1.342 **AND** Nuclear YAP > −0.236 **AND** Cytobody Paxillin > 1.597

**Cellular state:** Adhesion-mature, mechanically tense, YAP-active mammary epithelial cells responding to EGF.

### Mechanistic narrative
1. High paxillin intensity = abundant, mature focal adhesions → integrin engagement activates FAK/Src → Grb2/SOS recruitment → Ras→ERK. Adhesion is a known *permissive license* for growth-factor-driven ERK.
2. Mature focal adhesions anchor actin stress fibers; dense F-actin (high cytoplasmic actin mean) both sustains adhesion tension and is itself required for ERK activation and nuclear translocation.
3. Actomyosin tension transmitted to the nucleus opens nuclear pores → YAP nuclear retention (YAP > −0.236).
4. Nuclear YAP/TAZ–TEAD transcribes **amphiregulin (AREG)**, an EGFR ligand → autocrine EGFR re-activation → *sustained* pERK; EGF–PI3K signaling reciprocally activates YAP — a feed-forward loop.
5. pERK phosphorylates paxillin (Ser126), FAK (Ser910), and myosin light chain kinase → actin remodeling and contractility → **closing a positive feedback loop**.

In this state, actin sits at the hub of a self-reinforcing adhesion–mechanotransduction–ERK circuit — precisely explaining why the MLP assigns actin its maximal attribution here.

### Category 1 — Directly confirms established literature
- **Adhesion and actin integrity are required for growth-factor ERK activation** (Aplin & Juliano, 1999; Renshaw et al., 1999; Schlaepfer et al., 1994; Aplin et al., 2001).
- **Paxillin is a direct ERK scaffold and substrate** (Ishibe et al., 2003; Ishibe et al., 2004).
- **Actin tension drives YAP nuclear localization** (Dupont et al., 2011; Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017; Aragona et al., 2013; Das et al., 2016).
- **ERK drives actin contractility via MLCK** — explains the *positive* actin–pERK correlation direction (Klemke et al., 1997).
- **Mammary-epithelial-specific:** ECM stiffness → integrin clustering → FAK/ERK (Paszek et al., 2005; Levental et al., 2009; Provenzano & Keely, 2011).

### Category 2 — New testable hypotheses
- **H1 (Dose-gating):** Actin–pERK coupling strength scales quantitatively with focal adhesion density. *Test:* Bin EGF-stimulated MCF10A cells by paxillin intensity; compute per-bin single-cell actin–pERK correlation; apply FAK inhibitor (PF-573228/defactinib) dose-response. *Prediction:* the correlation slope collapses with FAK inhibition, phenocopying the low-paxillin tree branches.
- **H2 (YAP as transcriptional amplifier):** Nuclear YAP licenses the coupling via AREG-EGFR feed-forward. *Test:* YAP/TAZ knockdown or verteporfin; measure single-cell actin–pERK coupling in paxillin-high cells; rescue with exogenous AREG. *Prediction:* YAP loss shifts cells toward the noisier Node 23-like regime; AREG restores it.
- **H3 (Paxillin-Ser126 as the molecular node):** *Test:* PXN CRISPR-KO with add-back of WT vs. S126A vs. phosphomimetic S126D. *Prediction:* S126A decouples actin attribution from pERK; S126D mimics the high-attribution state even at moderate adhesion.

## 3. SECONDARY ZONE — Node 24 (TP=38, Precision=90.5% — highest in tree)

**Logic:** Cytoplasm Paxillin > 1.342 **AND** Nuclear YAP ≤ −0.236 **AND** Cytoplasm Paxillin > 2.170

**Cellular state:** A rare subpopulation with *extreme* focal adhesion signal but YAP excluded from the nucleus.

### Mechanistic narrative
At extreme adhesion density, the **direct, transcription-independent integrin→FAK/Src→Grb2→Ras→ERK scaffold route** is sufficient — no YAP transcriptional amplification is needed. The actin–pERK coupling becomes nearly deterministic (90.5% precision). The contrast with sibling Node 23 (same YAP-low branch, paxillin 1.34–2.17, only 55.3% precision) indicates a **switch-like, threshold behavior**: coupling sharpens only beyond the extreme paxillin threshold. Together with Node 28, this reveals **two convergent roads** to the same actin–pERK coupling: YAP/AREG amplification (common) vs. brute-force adhesion scaffolding (rare but deterministic).

### Category 1 — Directly confirms established literature
- **Direct integrin→ERK wiring via FAK–Grb2, no transcription required** (Schlaepfer et al., 1994; Renshaw et al., 1999).
- **Physical paxillin–ERK association** provides the scaffold logic (Ishibe et al., 2003; 2004).
- **Adhesion size and YAP localization are dissociable** — YAP stays cytoplasmic when actin tension is insufficient despite adhesions being present (Dupont et al., 2011), consistent with observing a paxillin-extreme/YAP-low population.

### Category 2 — New testable hypotheses
- **H4 (Threshold switch):** The actin–pERK coupling turns on nonlinearly at extreme paxillin. *Test:* Fine-grained binning of paxillin intensity with sigmoid fitting; move cells across the threshold by titrating ECM ligand density or integrin-β1 blocking antibody (AIIB2). *Prediction:* a sharp inflection in actin–pERK correlation, not a linear ramp.
- **H5 (YAP-independence of the extreme-adhesion route):** *Test:* YAP knockout or TEAD inhibition in Node-24-state cells. *Prediction:* actin–pERK coupling is preserved (unlike Node 28), but is abolished by FAK/Src inhibition (PP2). Live ERK-KTR imaging (per Albeck et al., 2013) should show acute, adhesion-gated pERK pulses insensitive to verteporfin.
- **H6 (Structural basis):** Extreme paxillin likely reflects a ventral stress-fiber/focal-adhesion belt. *Test:* low-dose latrunculin B (actin integrity) vs. blebbistatin (contractility). *Prediction:* latrunculin abolishes the coupling; blebbistatin has weaker effect here than in the Node 28 state (where tension feeds YAP). **Rigor caveat:** gate on nuclear morphology/DAPI to exclude doublets or segmentation artifacts at extreme intensity values.

**Key publications:** Schlaepfer et al., *Nature* 1994; Renshaw et al., *J Cell Biol* 1999; Ishibe et al., *Mol Cell* 2003/2004; Dupont et al., *Nature* 2011; Hynes, *Cell* 2002; Turner, *Nat Cell Biol* 2000; Deakin & Turner, *J Cell Sci* 2008; Albeck et al., *Mol Cell* 2013.

## 4. Supporting Observations from Weaker Zones
- **Node 14** (paxillin 0.896–1.106, YAP > 0.586; 51.8%): at sub-threshold adhesion, *high* nuclear YAP partially compensates — suggesting functional redundancy between the adhesion-scaffold and YAP-transcriptional axes. Exploratory only.
- **Nodes 29/30** (DAPI split): G2-like (high-DAPI) cells show cleaner coupling (71.5% vs 59.2%), consistent with cell-cycle-structured ERK pulse activity (Albeck et al., 2013). Tertiary modifier.

## 5. Caveats
Attribution ≠ causation — all hypotheses require the perturbation tests above. Thresholds are in standardized units and should be mapped back to absolute intensities. Extreme-value leaves (Node 24) warrant artifact exclusion before biological interpretation.

**Bottom line:** The tree reveals that actin predicts pERK only when the adhesion–mechanotransduction machinery is engaged. Paxillin-rich focal adhesions are the master license; nuclear YAP is a parallel amplifier. Node 28 captures the common YAP-reinforced loop; Node 24 captures a rare, deterministic, YAP-independent adhesion-scaffold route — two experimentally separable mechanisms converging on the same actin–ERK circuit.
